after the defendant filed an anti-SLAPP motion to dismiss, Giacovas amended the complaint to 
add highly complex "civil conspiracy" claims, forcing the defense to incur massive costs to 
amend their defensive filings.1 Giacovas also allegedly lied in appellate briefs to the Ninth 
Circuit, falsely claiming the defendant was paid $14,000 for her investigation, despite sworn 
deposition testimony proving the payment was only $1,500 to $2,500.1 
Judicial Penalties and "Bio Scrubbing" 
The Medifast litigation ended in a total failure for Giacovas. In March 2011, the District Court 
dismissed all claims under the anti-SLAPP statute, a ruling fully upheld by the Ninth Circuit in 
2014.1 Given the malicious nature of the litigation, the court entered a judgment on April 20, 
2015, ordering Giacovas's client to pay a devastating $198,877.50 in attorneys' fees and costs.1 
Despite losing every claim, losing the appeal, and triggering a nearly $200,000 sanction 
against his client, Giacovas engaged in what critics termed "bio scrubbing".1 He explicitly listed 
the Medifast defamation lawsuit as a "representative matter" and a "big win" on the Lazare 
Potter & Giacovas firm website.1 This deliberate misrepresentation of a catastrophic legal failure 
to deceive prospective clients about his professional acumen perfectly encapsulates the 
ethical elasticity Bleich relies upon to prosecute the 13 Harrison Street litigation.1 
9. The Anti-SLAPP Counter-Offensive: Defending 
Code Compliance 
Faced with Bleich and Giacovas's extortionate litigation tactics, the defense strategy 
coordinated by Damerau and the Condominium Board correctly targets the fundamental flaw 
in the plaintiffs' methodology: the lawsuit seeks to penalize lawful code-compliance 
enforcement.1 By utilizing New York's amended Anti-SLAPP statutes (CPLR 3211(g) and Civil 
Rights Law § 76-a), the defense seeks not only dismissal but mandatory financial penalties 
against Bleich.1 
Reframing the Dispute: Code Compliance as a "Public Interest" 
Under New York Civil Rights Law § 76-a(1)(a), an "action involving public petition and 
participation" includes claims based upon communications in a public forum or any lawful 
conduct in furtherance of the constitutional right to petition in connection with an issue of 
public interest.1 The 2020 amendments to the statute mandate that "public interest" must be 
"construed broadly" to mean "any subject other than a purely private matter".1 
The Bleich lawsuit attempts to frame the dispute as a private internal governance issue.1 
However, Justice Rosado's preliminary injunction decision explicitly recognized that Bleich's 
rooftop HVAC equipment lacks a permit and violates Department of Buildings (DOB) 
regulations, and that Article VI § 11(d) of the Condominium By-Laws legally obligates the Board
